transcription.tex: This chapter applies first- and second-order differential equations in practical settings.
1. First-order modelling\par A particle has acceleration \(a=t+3v/t\), \(t>0\), and \(v=0\) when \(t=2\). Show \(v=ct^3-t^2\), finding \(c\).
2. Simple harmonic motion\par Acceleration towards a central point is proportional to displacement:\[\ddot x=-\omega^2x.\]
3. Damped and forced harmonic motion\par Model damping forces and additional external forces.
4. Coupled first-order equations\par Differential-equation versions of simultaneous equations, including population models:\[\dot x=ax+by,\quad\dot y=cx+dy.\]

transcription.tex: Pure Year 2 introduced forming and solving first-order models. Here these may have the form \(y^{\prime}+Py=Q\). Motion gives examples such as \(a=dv/dt\).

A particle \(P\) starts from rest at a point \(O\) and moves along a straight line. At time \(t\) seconds the acceleration, \(a\) ms-2, of \(P\) is given by\par \(a=\frac{6}{{\left(t+2\right)}^{2}},\hspace{0.56em}t\ge 0\)\par (a) Find the velocity of \(P\) at time \(t\) seconds.\par (b) Show that the displacement of \(P\) from \(O\) when \(t=6\) is \((18-12\ln 2)\)m
\[\frac{dv}{dt}=\frac6{(t+2)^2}\Rightarrow v=-\frac6{t+2}+c.\]\[v(0)=0\Rightarrow c=3\Rightarrow v=3-\frac6{t+2}.\]
A particle has acceleration \(a=t+3v/t\), \(t>0\). Given \(v(2)=0\), show \(v=ct^3-t^2\), finding \(c\).\par Hint: write in the form \(dv/dt+Pv=Q\) and multiply by \(e^{\int P\,dt}\).
\[\frac{dv}{dt}-\frac3tv=t\]\[\mathrm{IF}=e^{\int-3/t\,dt}=e^{-3\ln t}=t^{-3}\]\[\frac d{dt}(t^{-3}v)=t^{-2}\]\[t^{-3}v=-t^{-1}+c.\]\[v(2)=0\Rightarrow c=\tfrac12\]\[v=\tfrac12t^3-t^2.\]

transcription.tex: A tank initially contains 1000 litres of pure water. Liquid leaves at 30 litres/hour and solution enters at 40 litres/hour, containing 4 grams of copper sulphate per litre. It mixes immediately throughout the tank. Let \(x\) be the copper sulphate mass in grams after \(t\) hours.\par (a) Show \(dx/dt=160-3x/(100+t)\).\par (b) Find the mass after 6 hours.\par (c) Explain how the model could be refined.

Volume: \(1000+40t-30t=1000+10t\) litres.\par Concentration: \(x/(1000+10t)\) g/litre.\par Inflow: \(40\times4=160\) g/hour.\par Outflow: \(30x/(1000+10t)=3x/(100+t)\) g/hour.\[\frac{dx}{dt}=160-\frac{3x}{100+t}.\]
Allow for the time taken for the copper sulphate to disperse, instead of assuming instantaneous mixing.

transcription.tex: Question 5

A sports car moves along a horizontal straight road. At time $t$ seconds the acceleration, in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, is modelled using the differential equation $\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dt}-2vt=t$ where $v$ is the velocity of the car in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. When $t=0$, the car is travelling at $1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.\par (a) Show that the velocity of the car at time $t$ seconds can be written as $v=\frac12(3\mathrm e^{t^2}-1)$.\par (b) Find the velocity of the car after 2 seconds.\par (c) State, with a reason, whether the model is suitable when $t=4$ seconds.

(a) Multiplying by the integrating factor $\mathrm e^{-t^2}$ gives $(v\mathrm e^{-t^2})'=t\mathrm e^{-t^2}$.\par Put $u=-t^2$. Integration gives $v\mathrm e^{-t^2}=-\tfrac12\mathrm e^{-t^2}+C$.\par At $t=0$, $1=-\tfrac12+C$, so $C=\tfrac32$ and $v=\tfrac12(3\mathrm e^{t^2}-1)$.
(c) $v(4)=\tfrac12(3\mathrm e^{16}-1)\approx1.33\times10^7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. A car cannot travel at this speed, so the model is unsuitable.

transcription.tex: Question 6

A raindrop falls vertically from rest through mist. Water condenses on the raindrop as it falls. You are given that the motion of the raindrop may be modelled by the equation $(t+4)\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dt}+4v=9.8(t+4)$ where $t$ is the time in seconds and $v$ is the velocity of the raindrop in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.\par (a) Show that $v=\frac{49(t+4)^5-c}{25(t+4)^4}$ where $c$ is a constant to be found.\par (b) Find the velocity of the raindrop after 5 seconds.\par (c) By considering the velocity for large values of $t$, suggest one criticism of the model.

(a) Divide by $t+4$. The integrating factor is $\exp\!\int\frac4{t+4}\,\mathrm dt=(t+4)^4$.\par $[v(t+4)^4]'=9.8(t+4)^4$, so $v(t+4)^4=\frac{49}{25}(t+4)^5+C$.\par Write $c=-25C$. At $t=0$, $v=0$, hence $c=49\cdot4^5=50176$.\par $v=\dfrac{49(t+4)^5-50176}{25(t+4)^4}$.
(c) $v\sim\frac{49}{25}(t+4)$ as $t\to\infty$. The model predicts a velocity that increases without limit.

transcription.tex: Question 7

A gas storage tank initially contains $500\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of helium. The helium leaks out at a constant rate of $20\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ per hour and a gas mixture is added to the tank at a constant rate of $50\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ per hour. The gas mixture contains 5% oxygen and 95% helium. Given that there is $x\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of oxygen in the tank after $t$ hours and that the oxygen immediately mixes throughout the tank on entry,\par (a) show that the situation can be modelled by the differential equation $\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=2.5-\frac{2x}{50+3t}$\par (b) Hence find the volume of oxygen in the tank after 4 hours.\par (c) Explain how the model could be refined.

(a) Oxygen enters at $0.05\times50=2.5\,\mathrm{cm^3\,h^{-1}}$. The volume of gas is $500+30t$.\par The oxygen fraction is $x/(500+30t)$. Therefore\par $\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=2.5-\frac{20x}{500+30t}=2.5-\frac{2x}{50+3t}$.
(c) Allow time for the oxygen to mix throughout the tank. Its concentration near the outlet may differ from the average concentration.

transcription.tex: \(O\) is the centre of oscillation. Moving away from \(O\), the particle slows down because its acceleration is towards \(O\). Doubling displacement doubles acceleration magnitude. It is not constant as in uniform gravity.

Simple harmonic motion (SHM) has acceleration towards a fixed point on the line of motion, proportional to displacement from that point:\[\ddot x=-\omega^2x.\]Dots mean time derivatives; \(\ddot x\) is acceleration. The minus sign makes it restoring. \(\omega>0\) is angular frequency in radians/second, and \(\omega^2\) the proportionality constant.\par The chain rule gives\[\ddot x=\frac{dv}{dt}=\frac{dv}{dx}\frac{dx}{dt}=v\frac{dv}{dx}.\]This helps solve the motion equation.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: A particle has SHM about \(O\), with maximum displacement \(a\).\par (a) Show \(v^2=\omega^2(a^2-x^2)\).

\[\ddot x=-\omega^2x\Rightarrow v\frac{dv}{dx}=-\omega^2x\]\[\int v\,dv=-\int\omega^2x\,dx\]\[\tfrac12v^2=-\tfrac12\omega^2x^2+c.\]At maximum displacement \(x=a\), \(v=0\), so \(c=\tfrac12\omega^2a^2\).\[\tfrac12v^2=-\tfrac12\omega^2x^2+\tfrac12\omega^2a^2\]\[v^2=\omega^2(a^2-x^2).\]
Complex numbers provide a practical tool for solving this applied motion equation.
(b) Show \(x=a\sin(\omega t+\alpha)\), with arbitrary phase \(\alpha\).

\[\ddot x+\omega^2x=0,\quad m^2+\omega^2=0\]\[m=\pm i\omega\Rightarrow x=A\cos\omega t+B\sin\omega t\]\[=R\sin(\omega t+\alpha).\]Using Pure Year 2 trigonometry, \(R=\sqrt{A^2+B^2}\). Since the amplitude is \(a\),\[x=a\sin(\omega t+\alpha).\]

Displacement follows a sine wave. Amplitude is maximum displacement. The phase \(\alpha\) controls translation; \(\alpha=0\) starts at equilibrium. Period \(T=2\pi/\omega\); \(\omega=1\) gives one oscillation per \(2\pi\) seconds.

transcription.tex: A particle is moving along a straight line. At time \(t\) seconds its displacement, \(x\) m from a fixed point \(O\) is such that \(\frac{{d}^{2}x}{d{t}^{2}}=-4x\).\par Given that at \(t=0, x=1\) and the particle is moving with velocity 4 ms-1,\par (a) find an expression for the displacement of the particle after \(t\) seconds\par (b) hence determine the maximum displacement of the particle from \(O\).\par Hint: find constants in the sine/cosine form before combining.
\[\ddot x+4x=0\Rightarrow m^2+4=0\Rightarrow m=\pm2i\]\[x=A\cos2t+B\sin2t.\]\[x(0)=1\Rightarrow A=1\]\[v=-2\sin2t+2B\cos2t\]\[v(0)=4\Rightarrow B=2\]\[x=\cos2t+2\sin2t.\]
\[x=\sqrt5\sin(2t+0.4636\ldots).\]Maximum displacement is \(\sqrt5\) m.

A particle \(P\), is attached to the ends of two identical elastic springs. The free ends of the springs are attached to two points \(A\) and \(B\). The point \(C\) lies between \(A\) and \(B\) such that \(ABC\) is a straight line and \(AC\ne BC\). The particle is held at \(C\) and then released from rest.\par At time \(t\) seconds, the displacement of the particle from \(C\) is \(x\) m and its velocity is \(v\) ms-1. The subsequent motion of the particle can be described by the differential equation \(\ddot{x}=-25x\).\par (a) Describe the motion of the particle.\par Given that \(x=0.4\) and \(v=0\) when \(t=0\),\par (b) solve the differential equation to find \(x\) as a function of \(t\)\par (c) state the period of the motion and calculate the maximum speed of \(P\).
Simple harmonic motion.
\[m^2+25=0\Rightarrow m=\pm5i\]\[x=A\cos5t+B\sin5t,\quad A=0.4\]\[v=-2\sin5t+5B\cos5t,\quad B=0\]\[x=0.4\cos5t.\]
\[T=\frac{2\pi}5\text{ s},\quad v=-2\sin5t.\]Maximum speed is \(2\) m s\(^{-1}\).

transcription.tex: Question 1

A particle is moving along a straight line. At time $t$ seconds its displacement, $x\,\mathrm m$, from a fixed point $O$ is such that $\frac{\mathrm d^2x}{\mathrm dt^2}=-9x$.\par (a) Describe the motion of the particle.\par Given that at $t=0$, $x=2$ and the particle is moving with velocity $3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$,\par (b) find an expression for the displacement of the particle after $t$ seconds.\par (c) Hence determine the maximum distance of the particle from $O$.
(a) The particle moves with simple harmonic motion about $O$.
(b) $m^2+9=0$ gives $m=\pm3i$, so $x=A\cos3t+B\sin3t$.\par $x(0)=2$ gives $A=2$. Since $\dot x=-3A\sin3t+3B\cos3t$, $\dot x(0)=3$ gives $B=1$.\par $x=2\cos3t+\sin3t$.
(c) Write $x=R\sin(3t+\alpha)$. Then $R\sin\alpha=2$, $R\cos\alpha=1$.\par The maximum distance is $R=\sqrt{2^2+1^2}=\sqrt5\,\mathrm m$.

sourceMapping.method: Typeset from the printed exam-style question and matched SolutionBank working.

transcription.tex: Question 2

A particle is moving with simple harmonic motion. After $t$ seconds its displacement, $x\,\mathrm m$ from a fixed point $O$ is such that $\ddot x=-16x$. Given that at $t=0$, $x=5$ and $\dot x=2$,\par (a) find an expression for the displacement of the particle after $t$ seconds.\par (b) Hence determine the period of motion and the maximum distance of the particle from $O$.
(a) $m^2+16=0$ gives $m=\pm4i$, so $x=A\cos4t+B\sin4t$.\par $x(0)=5$ gives $A=5$. Differentiating, $\dot x(0)=4B=2$.\par $x=5\cos4t+\tfrac12\sin4t$.
(b) $4T=2\pi$, so the period is $\pi/2$ seconds.\par Writing $x=R\sin(4t+\alpha)$ gives $R^2=5^2+(1/2)^2$. The maximum distance is $\tfrac{\sqrt{101}}2\,\mathrm m$.

sourceMapping.method: Typeset from the printed exam-style question and matched SolutionBank working.

transcription.tex: Question 3

A particle moves along a straight line. The particle moves such that its acceleration, in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, acts towards a fixed point $O$ and is proportional to its distance, $x\,\mathrm m$, from $O$.\par (a) Describe the motion of the particle.\par Given that the acceleration of the particle is $-5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ when $x=1$,\par (b) write down a differential equation to describe the motion of the particle.\par If the velocity and displacement of the particle at time $t=0$ are $6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $5\,\mathrm m$ respectively,\par (c) find an expression for the displacement of the particle after $t$ seconds.\par (d) Hence find the maximum distance of the particle from $O$.
(a) The particle moves with simple harmonic motion about $O$.
(b) $\ddot x=-kx$; at $x=1$ the acceleration is $-5$. Thus $k=5$ and $\ddot x=-5x$.
(c) $m^2+5=0$ gives $m=\pm i\sqrt5$. Write $x=A\cos(\sqrt5\,t)+B\sin(\sqrt5\,t)$.\par At $t=0$, $A=5$ and $\sqrt5 B=6$.\par $x=5\cos(\sqrt5\,t)+\tfrac6{\sqrt5}\sin(\sqrt5\,t)$.
(d) The maximum distance is the amplitude $\sqrt{5^2+(6/\sqrt5)^2}=\sqrt{161/5}\,\mathrm m$.

sourceMapping.method: Typeset from the printed exam-style question and matched SolutionBank working.

transcription.tex: Question 4

A particle moves along a straight line such that its acceleration, in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, acts towards a fixed point $O$ and is proportional to its distance, $x\,\mathrm m$, from $O$. The equation of motion is given as $\frac{\mathrm d^2x}{\mathrm dt^2}=-kx,\ t\geqslant0$ where $k$ is a constant. Given that the acceleration is $-7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ when $x=2$,\par (a) write down the value of $k$.\par (b) Use your answer to part a to find $x$ as a function of $t$ given that $x=6$ and $\dot x=1$ at time $t=0$.\par (c) Hence find, correct to 2 decimal places, the period of the motion.

(b) Write $\omega=\sqrt{7/2}$. The auxiliary roots are $\pm i\omega$, giving $x=A\cos\omega t+B\sin\omega t$.\par $x(0)=6$ gives $A=6$ and $\dot x(0)=\omega B=1$.\par $x=6\cos(\sqrt{7/2}\,t)+\sqrt{2/7}\sin(\sqrt{7/2}\,t)$.

sourceMapping.method: Typeset from the printed exam-style question and matched SolutionBank working.

transcription.tex: Question 5

A small rowing boat is floating on the surface of the sea, tied to a pier. The boat moves up and down in a vertical line, such that the vertical displacement, $x\,\mathrm m$, from its equilibrium point satisfies the equation $\frac{\mathrm d^2x}{\mathrm dt^2}=-2.25x,\ t\geqslant0$. Given that the maximum displacement is $1.3\,\mathrm m$ and it occurs when $t=2$ seconds,\par (a) find an expression for $x$ in terms of $t$ in the form $x=A\sin\omega t+B\cos\omega t$ where $A$, $B$ and $\omega$ are constants to be found. Give $A$ and $B$ correct to three decimal places.\par (b) State the time elapsed between the boat being at its highest and lowest points.\par (c) Criticise the model in terms of the motion of the boat for large values of $t$.

(a) $m^2+2.25=0$ gives $\omega=1.5$. Write $x=A\sin1.5t+B\cos1.5t$.\par At $t=2$, $A\sin3+B\cos3=1.3$ and $1.5A\cos3-1.5B\sin3=0$.\par Thus $A=1.3\sin3=0.183$ and $B=1.3\cos3=-1.287$ (3 d.p.).\par $x\approx0.183\sin1.5t-1.287\cos1.5t$.
(b) $T=2\pi/1.5=4\pi/3$. Highest to lowest takes half a period, $2\pi/3$ seconds.
(c) The model predicts the same highest and lowest points indefinitely. In reality the motion of the sea changes.

transcription.tex: Question 6

A particle $P$ is attached to one end of a light elastic spring. The other end of the spring is fixed to a point $A$ on the smooth horizontal surface on which $P$ rests. The particle is held at rest with $AP=0.9\,\mathrm m$ and then released. At time $t$ seconds the displacement of the particle from $A$ is $x\,\mathrm m$. The motion of the particle can be modelled using the equation $\ddot x=-200x$.\par (a) State the type of motion exhibited by the particle $P$.\par Given that $x=0.3$ and the particle is at rest when $t=0$,\par (b) solve the differential equation to find $x$ as a function of $t$\par (c) find the period and amplitude of the motion\par (d) calculate the maximum speed of $P$.
(a) Simple harmonic motion.
(b) $m^2+200=0$, so $\omega=10\sqrt2$. Write $x=A\cos\omega t+B\sin\omega t$.\par Using the given $x(0)=0.3$ gives $A=0.3$. Rest gives $\dot x(0)=\omega B=0$.\par $x=0.3\cos(10\sqrt2\,t)$.
(c) $T=\frac{2\pi}{10\sqrt2}=\frac{\pi\sqrt2}{10}\,\mathrm s$. The amplitude is $0.3\,\mathrm m$.
(d) $\dot x=-3\sqrt2\sin(10\sqrt2\,t)$. Maximum speed $=3\sqrt2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

sourceMapping.method: Typeset from the printed exam-style question and matched SolutionBank working.

transcription.tex: Question 7

A particle $P$ is attached to one end of a light elastic spring. The other end of the spring is fixed to a point $O$ on the smooth horizontal surface on which $P$ rests with $OP=2.6\,\mathrm m$ and then released. The motion of $P$ can be described using the equation $\ddot x=-\frac{100}{0.64}x$, where $x\,\mathrm m$ is the displacement of $P$ from $O$ at time $t$ seconds. Given that $x=1$ and the particle is at rest at time $t=0$,\par (a) solve the differential equation to find $x$ as a function of $t$\par (b) find the period of motion.
(a) $m^2+100/0.64=0$ gives $\omega=12.5$. Hence $x=A\cos12.5t+B\sin12.5t$.\par $x(0)=1$ gives $A=1$; rest gives $12.5B=0$. Therefore $x=\cos12.5t$.
(b) $12.5T=2\pi$, so $T=4\pi/25$ seconds.

sourceMapping.method: Typeset from the printed exam-style question and matched SolutionBank working.

transcription.tex: Question 8

A smooth cylinder is fixed with its axis horizontal. A piston of mass $2.5\,\mathrm{kg}$ is inside the cylinder, attached to one end of the cylinder by a spring of natural length $50\,\mathrm{cm}$. The piston is held at rest in the cylinder with the spring compressed to a length of $42\,\mathrm{cm}$. The piston is then released. The spring can be modelled as a light elastic spring and the piston can be modelled as a particle. The motion of $P$ can be described using the equation $\ddot x=-320x$, where $x\,\mathrm{cm}$ is the compression of the spring from its natural length at time $t$ seconds. Given that $x=8$ and $v=0$ when $t=0$,\par (a) solve the differential equation to find $x$ as a function of $t$\par (b) find the period of the resulting oscillations.
(a) $m^2+320=0$ gives $\omega=8\sqrt5$. Thus $x=A\cos\omega t+B\sin\omega t$.\par $x(0)=8$ gives $A=8$ and $\dot x(0)=0$ gives $B=0$. Hence $x=8\cos(8\sqrt5\,t)$ cm.
(b) $T=\frac{2\pi}{8\sqrt5}=0.351\,\mathrm s$ (3 d.p.).

sourceMapping.method: Typeset from the printed exam-style question and matched SolutionBank working.

transcription.tex: Question 9

A pendulum $P$ is attached to one end of a light inextensible string. The other end of the string is attached to a fixed point $A$ on a ceiling. The pendulum hangs in equilibrium at a point $B$ vertically below $A$. The pendulum is then moved through a horizontal distance of $15\,\mathrm{cm}$ and released from rest. The subsequent motion can be modelled using the equation $\ddot x=-\frac{250}{3}x$ where $x\,\mathrm{cm}$ is the horizontal displacement from the vertical at time $t$ seconds and $t\geqslant0$.\par (a) Solve the differential equation to find $x$ as a function of $t$.\par (b) Find the period and amplitude of the motion.\par Anton says that since the pendulum describes simple harmonic motion, the model suggests that the pendulum will stay swinging forever.\par (c) Suggest a refinement of the model in light of this statement.

(a) $m^2+250/3=0$ gives $\omega=\sqrt{250/3}$. Hence $x=A\cos\omega t+B\sin\omega t$.\par Taking the initial displacement as positive, $x(0)=15$ and $\dot x(0)=0$, so $A=15$, $B=0$.\par $x=15\cos(\sqrt{250/3}\,t)$ cm.
(b) $T=2\pi/\sqrt{250/3}=0.688\,\mathrm s$ (3 d.p.). The amplitude is $15\,\mathrm{cm}$.
(c) Include damping from air resistance so that the amplitude decreases with time.

transcription.tex: In practice the amplitude often decreases over time. Damping opposes velocity and its magnitude is proportional to speed.\par The spring’s elastic force is called the restoring force.
Without damping, spring extension or compression gives a restoring acceleration proportional to displacement, resulting in sinusoidal motion.
With damping
\(\ddot x=-k\dot x-\omega^2x\)\par \(\ddot x+k\dot x+\omega^2x=0,\quad k>0.\)
The roots of the auxiliary equation determine the type of damped motion.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: \[\ddot x+k\dot x+\omega^2x=0,\quad k,\omega>0.\]\[m^2+km+\omega^2=0.\]The discriminant determines the nature of the roots.
Distinct real roots:\[k^2-4\omega^2>0\]
\[x=Ae^{-\alpha t}+Be^{-\beta t},\quad\alpha,\beta>0.\]
Heavy damping: no repeated oscillations.
Equal real roots:\[k^2-4\omega^2=0\]
Critical damping: the boundary between oscillatory and non-oscillatory motion.
Complex conjugate roots:\[k^2-4\omega^2<0\]
\[x=e^{-kt/2}(A\cos\Omega t+B\sin\Omega t)\]\[\Omega=\sqrt{\omega^2-k^2/4}.\]
Light damping: oscillations with decreasing amplitude.

transcription.tex: A particle \(P\) of mass 0.5 kg moves in a horizontal straight line. At time \(t\) seconds, the displacement of \(P\) from a fixed point, \(O\), on the line is \(x\) m and the velocity of \(P\) is \(v\) ms-1. A force of magnitude \(8x\) N acts on \(P\) in the direction \(PO\). The particle is also subject to a resistance of magnitude \(4v\) N. When \(t=0, x=1.5\) and \(P\) is moving in the direction of increasing \(x\) with speed \(4\) ms-1,\par (a) Show that \(\frac{{d}^{2}x}{d{t}^{2}}+8\frac{dx}{dt}+16x=0\)\par (b) Find the value of \(x\) when \(t=1\).

\[m^2+8m+16=0\Rightarrow m=-4\]\[x=(A+Bt)e^{-4t}.\]\[x(0)=1.5\Rightarrow A=1.5\]\[v=Be^{-4t}-4(A+Bt)e^{-4t}\]\[v(0)=4\Rightarrow B=10\]\[x=(1.5+10t)e^{-4t}\]\[x(1)=11.5e^{-4}\approx0.211\text{ m (3 s.f.)}.\]Equal roots give critical damping.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: A particle hangs in equilibrium on a light elastic string fixed at \(A\). It is pulled down into a resisting liquid and released from rest. While the string is taut and the particle remains submerged,\[\ddot x+6k\dot x+5k^2x=0,\quad k>0.\]Find the general solution and type of damping.
\[m^2+6km+5k^2=(m+5k)(m+k)=0\]\[m=-5k,-k\]\[x=Ae^{-5kt}+Be^{-kt}.\]Two distinct real roots give heavy damping.

A particle hangs in equilibrium from a light elastic spring fixed at \(A\). It is pulled down and released from rest, with resistance proportional to speed. Its displacement from equilibrium obeys\[\ddot x+2k\dot x+2k^2x=0,\quad k>0.\]Find the general solution and period of oscillation.

\[m^2+2km+2k^2=0\]\[m=\frac{-2k\pm\sqrt{4k^2-8k^2}}2=-k\pm ik\]\[x=e^{-kt}(A\cos kt+B\sin kt).\]\[T=\frac{2\pi}k.\]The coefficient of \(t\) in the sine/cosine gives the angular frequency of the oscillation.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: An additional external force produces forced harmonic motion:\[\ddot x+k\dot x+\omega^2x=f(t).\]This is non-homogeneous, so use CF + PI.\par A particle of mass 1.5 kg moves on the \(x\)-axis under restoring force \(-7.5x\) N, resistance \(-6\dot x\) N and external force \(12\sin t\) N in the positive direction. Initially \(x=5,\dot x=2\).\par (a) Show \(\ddot x+4\dot x+5x=8\sin t\).\par (b) Find \(x(t)\).\par (c) Describe the motion for large \(t\).
\[-7.5x-6\dot x+12\sin t=1.5\ddot x\]\[\ddot x+5x+4\dot x=8\sin t\]\[\ddot x+4\dot x+5x=8\sin t.\]
As \(t\to\infty\), \(e^{-2t}\to0\). Hence the transient decays and\[x\sim\sin t-\cos t=\sqrt2\sin(t-\pi/4).\]The limiting motion is SHM with amplitude \(\sqrt2\) m and period \(2\pi\) s.

\[m^2+4m+5=0\Rightarrow m=-2\pm i\]\[x_c=e^{-2t}(A\cos t+B\sin t).\]Try \(x_p=p\sin t+q\cos t\):\[\dot x_p=p\cos t-q\sin t,\quad\ddot x_p=-p\sin t-q\cos t.\]\[(-p\sin t-q\cos t)+4(p\cos t-q\sin t)\]\[+5(p\sin t+q\cos t)=8\sin t.\]\[p+q=0,\quad p-q=2\Rightarrow p=1,q=-1.\]\[x=e^{-2t}(A\cos t+B\sin t)+\sin t-\cos t.\]\[x(0)=5\Rightarrow A-1=5\Rightarrow A=6\]\[\dot x(0)=2\Rightarrow-2A+B+1=2\Rightarrow B=13\]\[x=e^{-2t}(6\cos t+13\sin t)+\sin t-\cos t.\]

transcription.tex: A particle \(P\) is attached to end \(A\) of a light elastic spring \(AB\). Initially the particle and the string lie at rest on a smooth horizontal plane. At time \(t=0\), the end \(B\) of the string is set in motion and moves with constant speed \(U\) in the direction \(AB\), and the displacement of \(P\) from \(A\) is \(x\). Air resistance acting on \(P\) is proportional to its speed. The subsequent motion can be modelled by the differential equation\par \(\frac{{d}^{2}x}{d{t}^{2}}+2k\frac{dx}{dt}+{k}^{2}x=2kU\)\par Find an expression for \(x\) in terms of \(U, k\) and \(t\)

For \(k\ne0\), the auxiliary equation is\[m^2+2km+k^2=(m+k)^2=0\]\[\mathrm{CF}=(A+Bt)e^{-kt}.\]Since the forcing is constant, try \(x_p=c\):\[\dot x_p=\ddot x_p=0,\quad k^2c=2kU\Rightarrow c=\frac{2U}k.\]\[x=(A+Bt)e^{-kt}+\frac{2U}k.\]\[x(0)=0\Rightarrow A=-\frac{2U}k\]\[\dot x=-k(A+Bt)e^{-kt}+Be^{-kt}\]\[\dot x(0)=0\Rightarrow0=-kA+B\Rightarrow B=-2U\]\[x=\left(-\frac{2U}k-2Ut\right)e^{-kt}+\frac{2U}k.\]\par If \(k=0\), then \(\ddot x=0\). Initial rest and \(x(0)=0\) give \(x(t)=0\).

transcription.tex: Question 3

A particle $P$ is moving in a straight line. At time $t$, the displacement of $P$ from a fixed point on the line is $x$. The motion of the particle is modelled by the differential equation $\frac{\mathrm d^2x}{\mathrm dt^2}+2\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}+6x=0$. When $t=0$, $P$ is at rest at the point where $x=1$.\par (a) Find $x$ as a function of $t$.\par The smallest value of $t$, $t>0$, for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest is $T$.\par (b) Find the value of $T$.

(a) $m^2+2m+6=0$ gives $m=-1\pm i\sqrt5$. Write $x=\mathrm e^{-t}(A\cos\omega t+B\sin\omega t)$, $\omega=\sqrt5$.\par $x(0)=1$ gives $A=1$; $\dot x(0)=-A+\omega B=0$ gives $B=1/\sqrt5$.\par $x=\mathrm e^{-t}[\cos(\sqrt5\,t)+\tfrac1{\sqrt5}\sin(\sqrt5\,t)]$.
(b) Differentiating gives $\dot x=-\frac6{\sqrt5}\mathrm e^{-t}\sin(\sqrt5\,t)$.\par The first positive zero is $T=\pi/\sqrt5\approx1.40$.

transcription.tex: Question 4

A particle $P$ is attached to one end of a light elastic spring. The other end of the spring is attached to a fixed point $A$ and $P$ hangs freely in equilibrium vertically below $A$. At time $t=0$, $P$ is projected vertically downwards with speed $u$. A resistance proportional to the speed of $P$ acts on $P$. The motion of $P$ can be modelled using the differential equation $\frac{\mathrm d^2x}{\mathrm dt^2}+4k\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}+4k^2x=0$ where $x$ is the displacement of $P$ from its equilibrium position at time $t$ and $k$ is a positive constant.\par (a) Find an expression for $x$ in terms of $u$, $t$ and $k$.\par (b) Find the time at which $P$ comes to instantaneous rest.
(a) $(m+2k)^2=0$ gives $x=(A+Bt)\mathrm e^{-2kt}$.\par $x(0)=0$ gives $A=0$. Then $\dot x=B(1-2kt)\mathrm e^{-2kt}$, so $B=u$.\par $x=ut\mathrm e^{-2kt}$.
(b) $\dot x=u(1-2kt)\mathrm e^{-2kt}=0$, so $t=1/(2k)$.

transcription.tex: Question 5

A particle of mass $2\,\mathrm{kg}$ moves in a horizontal straight line. At time $t$ seconds, the displacement of $P$ from a fixed point $O$ is $x$ metres and the speed of $P$ is $v\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. A force of magnitude $6x\,\mathrm N$ acts on $P$ in the direction $PO$. The particle is also subject to a resistance of magnitude $2v\,\mathrm N$. When $t=0$, $x=1$ and $P$ is moving in the direction of increasing $x$ with speed $2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.\par (a) Show that $\ddot x+\dot x+3x=0$.\par (b) Solve the differential equation in part a to find $x$ as a function of $t$.\par (c) Find the value of $x$ when $t=2$.\par (d) Describe the motion of $P$ for large values of $t$.
(a) The resultant force is $-6x-2\dot x$. Hence $2\ddot x=-6x-2\dot x$, giving $\ddot x+\dot x+3x=0$.

(b) $m^2+m+3=0$ gives $m=(-1\pm i\sqrt{11})/2$. Let $\omega=\sqrt{11}/2$.\par $x=\mathrm e^{-t/2}(A\cos\omega t+B\sin\omega t)$. At $t=0$, $A=1$ and $-A/2+B\omega=2$.\par $x=\mathrm e^{-t/2}[\cos(\omega t)+\tfrac5{\sqrt{11}}\sin(\omega t)]$.
(c) $x(2)=\mathrm e^{-1}[\cos\sqrt{11}+\tfrac5{\sqrt{11}}\sin\sqrt{11}]\approx-0.459\,\mathrm m$.
(d) The oscillations continue with exponentially decreasing amplitude. The displacement tends to zero.

transcription.tex: Question 6

A particle $P$ is attached to end $A$ of a light elastic spring $AB$. The end $B$ of the spring is oscillating. At time $t$ the displacement of $P$ from a fixed point is $x$. When $t=0$, $x=0$ and $\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=\frac k5$ where $k$ is a constant. Given that $x$ satisfies the differential equation $\frac{\mathrm d^2 x}{\mathrm dt^2}+9x=k\cos t$\par find $x$ as a function of $t$.

$m^2+9=0$ gives $x_c=A\cos3t+B\sin3t$. Try $x_p=C\cos t$: $8C=k$.\par $x=A\cos3t+B\sin3t+\tfrac k8\cos t$.\par $x(0)=0$ gives $A=-k/8$ and $\dot x(0)=k/5$ gives $3B=k/5$.\par $x=\tfrac k8(\cos t-\cos3t)+\tfrac{k}{15}\sin3t$.

transcription.tex: Question 7

A particle $P$ is attached to end $A$ of a light elastic spring $AB$. Initially the spring and the particle lie at rest on a horizontal surface. The end $B$ of the spring is then moved in a straight line in the direction $AB$ with constant speed $U$. As $P$ moves it is subject to a resistance proportional to its speed. The extension, $x$, in the spring can be modelled using the differential equation $\frac{\mathrm d^2x}{\mathrm dt^2}+5k\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}+6k^2x=5kU$\par Find an expression in $x$ in terms of $t$.

$(m+2k)(m+3k)=0$. A constant particular solution satisfies $6k^2x_p=5kU$.\par $x=A\mathrm e^{-2kt}+B\mathrm e^{-3kt}+5U/(6k)$. Initially the extension is zero and its rate of increase is $U$.\par $A+B=-5U/(6k)$ and $-2kA-3kB=U$ give $A=-3U/(2k)$ and $B=2U/(3k)$.\par $x=\tfrac{2U}{3k}\mathrm e^{-3kt}-\tfrac{3U}{2k}\mathrm e^{-2kt}+\tfrac{5U}{6k}$.

transcription.tex: Question 8

An engineering student is designing an oscillating piston that is attached to a vertical rod. The piston is to be released from rest from a point half way up the rod so that it oscillates in a vertical line. The vertical displacement, $x$ metres, of the top of the piston below its initial position at time $t$ seconds is modelled by the differential equation, $2\frac{\mathrm d^2x}{\mathrm dt^2}+3\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}+x=100\cos t,\ t\geqslant0$\par (a) Show that a particular solution to the differential equation is $x=30\sin t-10\cos t$\par (b) Hence find the general solution to the differential equation.\par (c) Use the model to find, to the nearest centimetre, the vertical distance of the top of the piston from its initial position 5 seconds after it is released.
(a) Try $x=C\cos t+D\sin t$. Substitution gives $(-C+3D)\cos t+(-3C-D)\sin t=100\cos t$.\par Therefore $-C+3D=100$, $D=-3C$, so $C=-10$, $D=30$.
(b) $2m^2+3m+1=(2m+1)(m+1)=0$. The complementary function is $A\mathrm e^{-t}+B\mathrm e^{-t/2}$.\par $x=A\mathrm e^{-t}+B\mathrm e^{-t/2}+30\sin t-10\cos t$.

(c) At release, $x(0)=0$ and $\dot x(0)=0$, so $A+B=10$, $2A+B=60$. Thus $A=50$, $B=-40$.\par $x(5)=50\mathrm e^{-5}-40\mathrm e^{-2.5}+30\sin5-10\cos5=-34.55\,\mathrm m$ (2 d.p.).\par The distance is $34.55\,\mathrm m$ above the initial position.

transcription.tex: Let \(x\) be the number of bears and \(y\) the number of fish at time \(t\). Each population’s rate of change depends on both populations.
Bears
\(\displaystyle \frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=a\,x+b\,y+f(t)\)
The fish term measures how prey availability contributes to the bear growth rate.
Fish
\(\displaystyle \frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=c\,x+d\,y+g(t)\)
More bears may cause a faster decline in fish numbers.
\(b\cdot y\) means “\(b\) times the number of fish”. In the survey on slide 44, \(b=0.1\) and \(c=-0.1\).

The coefficients \(a,b,c,d\) are constants. The functions \(f(t)\) and \(g(t)\) allow for time-dependent effects such as seasonal breeding. This simplified system is linear. The classical Lotka–Volterra predator–prey equations are nonlinear.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: The survey uses the populations from slide 43 with \(a=0.3,\ b=0.1,\ c=-0.1,\ d=0.5\). Here \(f(t)=g(t)=0\) for all \(t\), so the system is homogeneous.

At the start of the year 2010, a survey began on the numbers of bears and fish on a remote island in Northern Canada. After \(t\) years the number of bears, \(x\), and the number of fish, \(y\), on the island are modelled by the differential equations
Bears
\(\displaystyle \frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=0.3x+0.1y\)
More fish increase the bear growth rate.
Fish
\(\displaystyle \frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=-0.1x+0.5y\)
More bears decrease the fish growth rate.

\textbf{Method.} Make \(y\) the subject of the bear equation and differentiate. Substitute into the fish equation and solve the second-order equation for \(x\). Differentiate the result and use the first rearrangement to find \(y\).
\textbf{a} Show that \(\ddot x-0.8\dot x+0.16x=0\).
\[y=10\dot x-3x\Rightarrow\dot y=10\ddot x-3\dot x\]\[10\ddot x-3\dot x=-0.1x+0.5(10\dot x-3x)\]\[10\ddot x-8\dot x+1.6x=0\]\[\ddot x-0.8\dot x+0.16x=0.\]
\textbf{b} Find the general solution for the number of bears on the island at time \(t\).
\textbf{c} Find the general solution for the number of fish on the island at time \(t\).
\textbf{d} At the start of 2010 there were 5 bears and 20 fish on the island. Use this information to find the number of bears predicted to be on the island in 2020.
\textbf{e} Comment on the suitability of the model.
Both populations grow without limit, so this is unlikely to remain realistic.

transcription.tex: Two barrels contain contaminated water. At time \(t\) seconds, the amount of contaminant in barrel \(A\) is \(x\) ml and the amount of contaminant in barrel \(B\) is \(y\) ml. Additional contaminated water flows into barrel \(A\) at a rate of 5ml per second. Contaminated water flows from barrel \(A\) to barrel \(B\) and from barrel \(B\) to barrel \(A\) through two connecting hoses, and drains out of barrel \(A\) to leave the system completely.\par The system is modelled using the differential equations\par \(\frac{dx}{dt}=5+\frac{4}{9}y-\frac{1}{7}x\hspace{1.4em}\left(1\right)\)\par \(\frac{dy}{dt}=\frac{3}{70}x-\frac{4}{9}y\hspace{3.08em}(2)\)\par Show that \(630\frac{{d}^{2}y}{d{t}^{2}}+370\frac{dy}{dt}+28y=135\)\par Hint: make \(x\) the subject in (2), differentiate and substitute into (1).

\[\dot y+\tfrac49y=\tfrac3{70}x\]\[x=\tfrac{70}3\dot y+\tfrac{280}{27}y\]\[\dot x=\tfrac{70}3\ddot y+\tfrac{280}{27}\dot y.\]Substitute into (1):\[\tfrac{70}3\ddot y+\tfrac{280}{27}\dot y=5+\tfrac49y-\tfrac17(\tfrac{70}3\dot y+\tfrac{280}{27}y)\]\[70\ddot y+\tfrac{280}9\dot y=15+\tfrac43y-10\dot y-\tfrac{40}9y\]\[630\ddot y+280\dot y=135+12y-90\dot y-40y\]\[630\ddot y+370\dot y+28y=135.\]

transcription.tex: Question 4

At the start of 2012, a survey began on the number of sand foxes and the number of meerkats on a remote desert island. After $t$ years, the number of sand foxes, $x$, and the number of meerkats, $y$, on the island are modelled by the differential equations $\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=0.2x+0.2y$, $\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=-0.5x+0.4y$\par (a) Show that $\frac{\mathrm d^2x}{\mathrm dt^2}-0.6\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}+0.18x=0$.\par (b) Show that the general solution for the number of sand foxes at time $t$ is $x=\mathrm e^{\alpha t}(A\cos\beta t+B\sin\beta t)$ where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants to be found.\par (c) Find the general solution for the number of meerkats at time $t$. Give your answer in the form $y=P\mathrm e^{\alpha t}(Q\cos\beta t+R\sin\beta t)$ where $P$ is a constant to be found and $Q$ and $R$ are functions of $A$ and $B$.\par (d) Given that there were initially 3 sand foxes and 111 meerkats on the island, during which year does the model predict that the meerkats die out?\par (e) How many sand foxes will there be when the meerkats die out?\par (f) Use your answers to parts d and e to comment on the model.
(a) From the first equation, $y=5x'-x$. Differentiate $x'=0.2x+0.2y$.\par $x''=0.2x'+0.2(-0.5x+0.4y)=0.6x'-0.18x$.
(b) $m^2-0.6m+0.18=0$ gives $m=0.3\pm0.3i$.\par $x=\mathrm e^{0.3t}(A\cos0.3t+B\sin0.3t)$, so $\alpha=\beta=0.3$.
(c) Substitute the expression for $x$ into $y=5x'-x$. Collecting sine and cosine terms gives\par $y=\tfrac12\mathrm e^{0.3t}[(A+3B)\cos0.3t+(B-3A)\sin0.3t]$.\par Thus $P=1/2$, $Q=A+3B$, $R=B-3A$.

(d) $x(0)=3$ gives $A=3$; $y(0)=111$ gives $3+3B=222$, so $B=73$.\par $y=\mathrm e^{0.3t}(111\cos0.3t+32\sin0.3t)$.\par For the first zero, $0.3t=\pi-\arctan(111/32)$, so $t=6.17$ years. This is during 2018.
(e) At the first zero of $y$, $x=\mathrm e^{0.3t}(3\cos0.3t+73\sin0.3t)\approx441$. The model predicts 441 sand foxes.
(f) The model gives plausible positive populations initially. It then predicts negative meerkat numbers, and later negative fox numbers, so it cannot model the populations in the long term.

transcription.tex: Question 5

A tank of water contains two different types of chemical that react with each other. The rates of change of each chemical can be modelled using the differential equations $\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=-3x+2y$, $\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=-2x+y$ where $x$ is the number of litres of chemical $X$ and $y$ is the number of litres of chemical $Y$ at time $t$ hours. Initially there is one litre of chemical $X$ and two litres of chemical $Y$ in the tank.\par (a) Show that the solutions to the differential equations can be written as $x=P\mathrm e^{-t}$, $y=Q\mathrm e^{-t}$ where $P$ and $Q$ are functions of $t$ to be found.\par (b) Find, correct to three significant figures, the amount of each chemical at time $t=2$ hours.\par (c) Use the model to describe what happens to the amount of each chemical as $t$ gets large.

(a) $y=(x'+3x)/2$. Differentiation and substitution give $x''=-3x'+2(-2x+y)=-2x'-x$.\par $(m+1)^2=0$ gives $x=(A+Bt)\mathrm e^{-t}$, hence $y=(A+\tfrac12B+Bt)\mathrm e^{-t}$.\par $x(0)=1$, $y(0)=2$ give $A=1$, $B=2$. Thus $P=1+2t$, $Q=2+2t$.
(c) Both $\mathrm e^{-t}$ and $t\mathrm e^{-t}$ tend to zero. Both chemical quantities tend to zero.

sourceMapping.method: Typeset from the printed exam-style question and matched SolutionBank working.

transcription.tex: Question 6

A freely hanging pendulum oscillates in both the $x$ and $y$ directions. At time $t$, the rates of change of the $x$ and $y$ displacements are given by the differential equations $\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=-4y$, $\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=4x$\par (a) Show that the pendulum describes simple harmonic motion in the $y$ direction.\par Given that the initial displacement of the pendulum is $x=4$ and $y=5$,\par (b) find the particular solutions to the system of differential equations.
(a) $y'=4x$, so $y''=4x'=-16y$. The acceleration is proportional to displacement and directed towards equilibrium. This is simple harmonic motion.
(b) $m^2+16=0$ gives $y=A\cos4t+B\sin4t$. Then $x=y'/4=-A\sin4t+B\cos4t$.\par At $t=0$, $A=5$, $B=4$. Thus $y=5\cos4t+4\sin4t$ and $x=4\cos4t-5\sin4t$.

transcription.tex: Question 7

Joanna is investigating how a harmful substance from pollution is absorbed by the human body. She finds that the substance enters the body in the bloodstream and is transferred between the blood and the bodily organs. The harmful substance is then expelled from the body through, for example, sweat. The amount of the substance in the blood, $x\,\mathrm{mg}$, and the organs, $y\,\mathrm{mg}$, at time $t$ days, can be modelled using the differential equations $\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=-0.03x+0.01y+50$, $\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=0.01x-0.03y$\par (a) Show that $\frac{\mathrm d^2x}{\mathrm dt^2}+0.06\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}+0.0008x=1.5$\par (b) Hence find the general solutions to the system of differential equations in the form $x=\mathrm{f}(t)$, $y=\mathrm{g}(t)$\par (c) Describe what happens to the amount of the substance in the blood and the organs as $t$ gets large.
(a) $y=100x'+3x-5000$, hence $y'=100x''+3x'$.\par Substitution gives $100x''+3x'=0.01x-0.03(100x'+3x-5000)$.\par Divide by 100 and rearrange: $x''+0.06x'+0.0008x=1.5$.

(b) $(m+0.04)(m+0.02)=0$. A constant particular integral satisfies $0.0008x_p=1.5$, giving $x_p=1875$.\par $x=A\mathrm e^{-0.04t}+B\mathrm e^{-0.02t}+1875$.\par Using $y=100x'+3x-5000$ gives $y=-A\mathrm e^{-0.04t}+B\mathrm e^{-0.02t}+625$.
(c) Both exponential terms decay to zero. The amount tends to $1875\,\mathrm{mg}$ in the blood and $625\,\mathrm{mg}$ in the organs.

sourceMapping.method: Typeset from the printed exam-style question and matched SolutionBank working.

transcription.tex: Question 8

A biologist is examining the rates of change of nutrients in both tree roots and the surrounding soil. Nutrients pass from the tree roots into the soil and from the soil into the tree roots. Nutrients also enter the system through both the roots and the soil and escape from the system in the same way. The biologist believes that the amount of nutrients in the roots, $x$, and the amount of nutrients in the soil, $y$, at time $t$ hours, can be modelled using the differential equations $\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=-2x+y+1$, $\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=4x+y+2$\par (a) Show that $\frac{\mathrm d^2x}{\mathrm dt^2}+\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}-6x=1$.\par (b) Find the general solutions to the system of differential equations.\par (c) Using your answers to part b, comment on the suitability of the biologist’s model.
(a) $y=x'+2x-1$, so $x''=-2x'+y'=-2x'+4x+y+2$.\par Substitution gives $x''=-x'+6x+1$, hence $x''+x'-6x=1$.

(b) $(m-2)(m+3)=0$, and a constant particular solution is $-1/6$.\par $x=A\mathrm e^{2t}+B\mathrm e^{-3t}-\tfrac16$. Substituting into $y=x'+2x-1$ gives\par $y=4A\mathrm e^{2t}-B\mathrm e^{-3t}-\tfrac43$.
(c) For positive initial nutrient quantities the growing $\mathrm e^{2t}$ term dominates. Both quantities increase without bound, making the model unsuitable in the long term.
